description: This is Team ByteAero from Chittagong, Bangladesh. Our team is Ahmad Zubayer (team leader and front-end developer), Kiyas Mahmud (backend developer), Rehenuma Promi ( scripting and vocals), Rohit Roy (research), Rahul (video editor) and Safayet (data analyst). We are building Earth Jukebox: Guardian of Dhaka, a browser game that turns NASA satellite heat maps into music so that anyone, including blind and low-vision players, can find dangerous heat by ear and learn how to cool their city.
summary: Earth Jukebox: Guardian of Dhaka is a game that lets you hear the heat in your city and learn how to cool it down. Every April, Dhaka gets dangerously hot, and the people who suffer most are those who cannot stay indoors: rickshaw pullers, street sellers and children walking to school. NASA satellites can see where the heat is, but only as coloured maps, which leave out people who are blind or find charts hard to read. Our solution turns NASA’s real satellite maps of Dhaka into music: hotter ground plays higher sitar notes, rain plays the tabla, and green areas play the flute. The idea: you play a child in Dhaka who follows the sound to find the hottest blocks, then plants trees, digs ponds and paints roofs white before a heat wave hits. Because it works offline in any browser and can be played fully with a screen reader, anyone can learn real climate science, feel that they can help, and see that cooler cities are possible. Next, we want to translate the game into Bangla, bring it into Dhaka classrooms and schools for blind students, add NASA’s city night-lights data, and let players protect other hot cities.
details:
HOW IT WORKS

Earth Jukebox: Guardian of Dhaka is a 3D game that runs in a web browser and turns NASA satellite data into music. You play a child in Dhaka who finds dangerous heat by listening to it. We took NASA's MODIS satellite maps of ground heat and green plants in Dhaka for April 2000, 2010, 2020 and 2024. Our program uses NASA's own colour key to turn each pixel back into a number, then averages those numbers over 25 city blocks. Each block then "plays" its data. Hotter ground plays higher sitar notes, rain (from NASA POWER) plays the tabla, and greener areas play the flute. The sound comes from the direction of the heat, so you can walk toward it by ear. When you find a hot spot, you spend a small budget on trees, white roofs, ponds or cooling centres before a heat wave arrives. After each year you get a report with the real NASA maps, a fact and a quick quiz. You play four real years and then two imagined futures (2035 and 2050) that your choices shape. At the end, all six years play back as one song, the Earth Record, which you can download.

TRY IT

Play it in any web browser, on a laptop or a phone. There's nothing to install and no sign-up.

https://nsac-26-byteaero-guardians-of-dhaka.vercel.app/
Source Code: https://github.com/AhmadZubayer/ByteAero-Earth-Jukebox-Guardian-of-Dhaka-NSAC-2026/tree/main

BENEFITS

  • You can hear the science. People who can't see or read a heat map can still find the heat.
  • It's built for accessibility. Every sound has a caption. There's a text-only mode for screen readers, a relaxed mode with no timer, reduced motion, and keyboard and touch controls.
  • It's light and works offline. It's about 4.5 MB and runs on a laptop or phone. It needs no internet after it loads.
  • It fits a classroom. Each year takes 3–4 minutes and ends with a report and a quiz.
  • It feels local. Rickshaws, tea stalls, mango and neem trees: people in Dhaka will recognise their own city.

IMPACT

We want children, families and teachers in Bangladesh, and anyone else, to understand why crowded concrete areas get dangerously hot and what can be done about it. Players learn that trees, water and light-coloured roofs help cool a city. They also learn that keeping people safe, such as with a cooling centre, is not the same as cooling the city. We want NASA's Earth data to be open to blind and low-vision people. We want players to learn honest science that even adults often mix up: the ground is not the air, and one hot year is not a trend. Above all, we want players to leave with hope, not fear. Even the hardest ending says it is "a warning, not a fate."

TOOLS

  • Languages: JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the game. TypeScript and React (Remotion) for the demo video.
  • Game libraries: three.js for 3D, the Web Audio API for all the music (made live in code, with no recorded tracks), GSAP for animation, postprocessing and three.quarks for visual effects, and nipplejs for the phone joystick.
  • Build and testing: Bun, Vite, Playwright for automated browser tests, glTF-Transform to shrink 3D models, and pngjs to read the NASA images.
  • Hosting and teamwork: GitHub and Vercel.
  • AI help: Claude Code (an AI coding assistant) helped write and test the code.
  • Assets: free CC0 3D models from Quaternius and KayKit, and a CC0 font by GGBotNet. The Dhaka buildings, rickshaws, tea stall and Echo the drone are built in code.
  • NASA data: MODIS land surface temperature and NDVI (GIBS/Worldview), NASA POWER, GISTEMP v4, SVS visualization 5060, and Blue Marble.
  • Hardware: ordinary laptops, with no special equipment. Our test laptop has AMD Ryzen built-in graphics and runs the game at about 60 frames per second.

CREATIVITY

  • Sound is how you play, not decoration. In 2020 the colours and the arrow disappear, and you must find the heat by ear alone.
  • The music sounds like home. It uses South Asian instruments and ragas. A tense scale plays when the city is hot, and the rain raga Megh Malhar plays in a rainy year.
  • The sound has direction. The sitar plays from where the heat is, and Echo's scan sweeps notes around you to point the way.
  • The music tells you how you did. A year you protected ends on a calm "home" note. A year left in the heat ends on an unfinished-sounding note.
  • A story ties it together. Echo picks up a broken message from a child in 2050, and each year you protect brings back one piece of it.
  • There's something to take home. You get your own song as a WAV file and a printable Earth Listener Ticket with badges.

CONSIDERATIONS

  • Science honesty: The street names are invented, but each block's heat is real NASA data. We explain that ground temperature is not air temperature and that four snapshots don't prove a trend. Cooling effects are labelled as game estimates, and 2035 and 2050 are clearly imagined. The music is inspired by NASA's sonification work; it is not official NASA audio.
  • Accessibility: captions, text-only mode, relaxed mode, reduced motion, and keyboard and touch controls.
  • Cheap phones and slow internet: a small download, no network use while playing, and a low-graphics setting.
  • Young players: simple words, one task at a time, a tutorial, and hints when you're stuck.
  • Local culture: Dhaka's streets, trees, food stalls, and music.
  • Hope over fear: every ending leaves room to act.
  • Real choices: a limited budget means players have to weigh costs and trade-offs.
  • Licences: NASA public-domain data, CC0 assets, and every source listed in our credits.
  • Testing: automated browser tests, including a bot that finds hidden heat by sound alone, plus a game-balance simulation.
